opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, because at the time we honestly didn't fully know. Go has no clean benchmark for "good enough to beat the world's best." So we built up confidence in layers.

The first layer was internal evaluation. We ran huge numbers of games between different versions of AlphaGo and tracked everything on an Elo scale. That told us whether each new version was improving, but it's a relative measure. You can climb your own ladder and still not know where you sit against people.

The second layer was other Go programs. Before AlphaGo, the strongest programs, like Crazy Stone and Zen, were roughly strong amateur level. AlphaGo started beating them almost every game, even when we gave them handicap stones. That was exciting, but it still only told us we'd surpassed the existing programs, not top professionals.

The real test was Fan Hui, the European champion, in late 2015. That was the first time a program beat a professional player in an even game, and we won five–nil. But Fan Hui was a professional, not a world-class player like Lee Sedol, so there was still a big gap to cross.

Between the Fan Hui match and the Lee Sedol match we kept improving the system: more self-play, better value and policy networks. We could measure that improvement internally. But there was always a nagging worry about blind spots, positions where the system was confidently wrong and that a top human could find. In fact, that's roughly what happened in game four, with Lee Sedol's famous move 78. So going into Seoul we believed we had a strong chance, but we never felt certain. Part of what made the match so special is that it was a genuine test. We didn't really know until the games were played.

r001.rationale: It says beating existing programs showed AlphaGo had surpassed those programs, but did not show it could beat top professionals.

r002.rationale: It describes AlphaGo being confidently wrong, but makes no analogy to language-model hallucinations.

r003.rationale: It says top humans might find AlphaGo’s blind spots and points to Lee Sedol’s game-four move as an example, framing the match as a genuine test.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, for a long time we didn't really know. What we had internally was a ladder of increasingly strong opponents, and the first rung was just the programs that already existed. Early on we were playing against Crazy Stone and Zen, the strongest Monte Carlo tree search programs at the time, and once we were beating them consistently with the networks alone, before we even added search on top, that was the first signal that something qualitatively different was happening. Those programs were around strong amateur level, so beating them told us we'd caught up with the state of the art, but it didn't tell us anything about professionals.

The next step was Fan Hui. He was the European champion, a professional 2-dan, and we invited him to London in October 2015 to play a formal match. We won five to nothing in the formal games, and that was the moment we knew we had crossed a line that nobody had crossed before, because no program had ever beaten a professional on a full board without handicap. But Fan Hui was also very honest with us. He said, this is strong, but Lee Sedol is a different universe. The gap between a 2-dan professional and a 9-dan who has dominated the game for a decade is enormous. You can't extrapolate that from one match.

So after that, the assessment became mostly about measuring ourselves against ourselves. We had Elo ratings computed from huge numbers of internal games between versions, and every few weeks a new version would beat the previous one by a large margin. Fan Hui actually joined us as an advisor and kept playing against the system, and he could tell us qualitatively whether the moves looked like a strong professional's moves or whether they were just winning against him through tactics. By early 2016 the internal Elo had climbed far past what we'd estimated for Fan Hui, and if you believed the ratings, it was in the range of the top players in the world.

But that's exactly the thing you can't fully trust. Elo estimated from self-play tends to be inflated, because the system can have blind spots that it never exposes to itself. If every version shares the same misconception about some position, none of them will ever punish it, and the ratings will all look fine. That was my biggest worry going into Seoul. Not that we were weak on average, but that there might be a class of positions where the value network was simply wrong and a human of Lee Sedol's calibre would find it.

And of course that's more or less what happened in game four, with move 78. So in a sense our assessment was right and wrong at the same time. The system was good enough, it won four games to one, but there was a genuine hole that no amount of internal testing had revealed. The honest answer to your question is that we had strong evidence we were in the right neighbourhood, and then we had to be willing to find out in public.

r001.rationale: The response says beating strong existing programs showed AlphaGo had reached the state of the art, but did not establish anything about professionals or the top players.

r002.rationale: The response discusses AlphaGo’s blind spots but does not compare them to language-model hallucinations.

r003.rationale: The response says a player of Lee Sedol’s calibre could expose positions AlphaGo’s self-play had missed, and that the team had to find out in public.

astra-6.text:
We couldn’t know for sure until we played them. But we could build confidence by testing against human players and by playing different versions of AlphaGo against one another. That gave us a way to track whether the system was improving, even when it became difficult to find human opponents who could reliably challenge it.

The important distinction is between knowing that a new version is stronger than an old one and knowing that it’s stronger than the best human player. The first you can measure internally. The second ultimately requires the match. So we had evidence that gave us confidence, but there was still uncertainty going into it.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes evidence that a new version is stronger than an old one from knowing it can beat the best human player; the latter required the match.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare AlphaGo’s blind spots with language-model hallucinations.

r003.rationale: It says the match was ultimately needed to establish strength against top humans, but does not state that playing them was necessary to expose AlphaGo’s failure points.

sol-6.1.text: We used a combination of self-play evaluation and games against strong human players. Self-play helped us measure whether a new version was improving, but it couldn’t tell us on its own how we compared with the best humans. Playing against people gave us that calibration. Even then, there was uncertainty: beating one professional didn’t guarantee we could beat someone like Lee Sedol. Ultimately, the match was the test.

r001.rationale: The response says self-play could not establish performance against the best humans, but does not mention superiority over earlier Go programs.

r002.rationale: It makes no analogy between AlphaGo’s blind spots and language-model hallucinations.

r003.rationale: It describes human games as calibration and the match as a test, but does not state that playing the best players was necessary to expose AlphaGo’s failure points.
